Ian Zepp — Cold starts, real engineering

 Autobiography / selected works / 1996—present

Cold starts. Real engineering.

I’m Ian Zepp — systems engineer, founder, former VP of Engineering. I learn unfamiliar technical domains from the ground up: asking the questions that surface real constraints, understanding the theory well enough to make design calls, then building engineering process robust enough to sustain AI-assisted development over months. This is the long version.

 Scroll to begin ↓

 What this is

Six case studies spanning 1999 to 2026. A seven-act career from the Marine Corps through real estate, enterprise platforms, founder exits, and full-time independent R&D. An evidence ledger graded A/B/C. The depth is below — the front door should reflect the scope.

 Currently building in Rust

 The thesis · 1996—present

Learn the domain. Verify the output.

The pattern started in 1999: write a KDE frontend for Nmap without knowing Qt, build a multi-tenant platform without knowing enterprise architecture, ship a Rust compiler without prior PL theory. Each time the approach is the same — learn the theory well enough to make real design calls, then build process robust enough that the output holds up under audit.

Since August 2025 that approach has run full time on AI-assisted systems: a programming language and its Rust compiler, a multi-agent runtime and fleet orchestration layer, a multi-tenant platform, MCP security tooling, and evaluation harnesses. The process came first — goals and invariants before code, work in bounded phases, completion audited apart from implementation — until the coordination load outgrew one person and the tooling was built to hand dispatch to agent fleets.

The case studies below trace the pattern across decades. The research programs, method, skills, and evidence ledger that follow are the current instantiation — deeper, more measured, but the same instinct that started in a barracks in 1999.

 Cold-starts domains
 From KDE protocol tools in 1999 to a Rust compiler without prior PL theory. The domain changes; the pattern doesn't.
 Rebuilds right when the context changes
 The same platform vision rebuilt clean-room across four iterations, two languages, and a decade. The design survived because it was correct.
 Builds the process before the code
 Goals and invariants first. Bounded phases. Audit apart from implementation. The loop runs by hand before it runs automated.
 Ships falsifiable systems
 Compilers, agent runtimes, operating systems, multi-tenant platforms. If it can't be tested, it doesn't count.
 Open source from day one
 Nmap citation in 1999, kdelibs contributor, 40+ public repositories. The work has always been inspectable.
 Evidence graded, not claimed
 Claims reconstructed against executed agreements, payroll records, and primary sources. Where the record is thin, the grade says so.

The sections below hold the proof: six case studies with dated metrics, six research programs with inspectable source, an operating method with named artifacts, a seven-act career reconstructed against primary records, and an evidence ledger graded A, B, or C depending on what the receipts support.

 The research programs

Six main lines of work.

Every program below is a running system with its own tests, documents, and Git history. Four satellites follow, and the archive at the bottom of the page holds the rest.

 Language / compiler · Active · private

Faber / Radix

A Latin-derived programming language and Radix, its Rust compiler: one semantic core with multiple locale renderings, HIR/MIR lowering, emission across Rust, Go, TypeScript, WebAssembly, LLVM, Metal, and WGSL. Built without prior PL-theory background—chosen because a compiler cannot bluff. Clippy pedantic at deny across every crate; structured release notes on a daily median cadence.

 281K LOC · 24 crates3,714 test functions59 releases · median 1 day
 faberlang.dev ↗github.com/faberlang ↗Grammar ↗

 Agent runtime · Active · private

Minted Geek Swarm

A Rust multi-agent runtime unifying mail, CRM, storage, payments, messaging, MCP tool servers, and LLM execution behind one authenticated HTTP boundary, with agent self-provisioning. Fleets coordinate by passing durable message handles rather than full context—session shape and cost structure moved when that layer landed.

 10.9M→2.5M tokens/session−61% cost per work-hour39 audit interventions · sample campaign
 mintedgeek.com ↗

 Seven-day build · Open source

Field Board

A real-time collaborative whiteboard with AI board manipulation, written in Rust end to end: Axum and PostgreSQL behind, Leptos and WebAssembly in front, binary protobuf frames between. Seven crates in seven days, February 2026.

 511 commits1,077 test definitions7 crates / 7 days
 Source ↗

 Evaluation science · Open + private

The Trials

Harnesses for asking whether models can actually learn Faber—grammar-only versus worked examples, n-shot matrices, three-level executable grading, judged drafter-and-reviewer pipelines—plus local-inference tuning, ethics-scenario designs, and blind design judging. One January study ran four models through 672 trials each.

 17,681 result rows26 models266 task definitions
 Harness ↗

 Programmable platform · Open source

Monk

A multi-tenant backend where the schema is data: model-first APIs, per-tenant isolation, observer rings, packages, cron—and protocol adapters that expose the same records over FUSE, FTP, and IRC. The clearest bridge between my enterprise-platform years and the current work.

 1,122 commits15+ ecosystem repos
 Source ↗

 Agent kernels · Mixed

The kernel lineage

A line of experiments in how agents should execute: Abbot’s persistent daemon, Prior’s typed frames and kernel routing, Muninn’s polyglot protocol family, Fleet’s Mind/Head/Hand orchestration—plus Cassio for transcript processing and Vivarium for email as a durable agent data surface.

 6 related systemsRust / TS / Go cores

 Satellites

 MCP security · collaborative

Cephalopodic

Gauntlet AI Cohort 4 capstone with two co-founders: a Go control plane and security gateway for MCP—registration, catalogs, user-scoped taps, policy enforcement, JSON-RPC inspection. Wound down within three months when managed MCP shipped natively and removed the market.

 Applied product

Gofolio

A Ghostfolio-compatible portfolio backend in Go, a Rust terminal client, and a live evaluation TUI running 73 defined cases across models with executable grading.

 Applied AI

LegacyLens

Retrieval-augmented analysis of legacy COBOL: custom parsing and chunking, vector indexing, hybrid retrieval, and natural-language answers over a real mainframe codebase.

 Research crate

QRStatic

Zero-dependency Rust steganography hiding QR codes in temporal noise correlation, with empirical codec, quantization, and recovery sweeps behind the defaults.

 The operating method

How the factory runs.

The loop below ran by hand for months before any of it was automated. Agents now supply throughput and tactical dispatch; problem definition and audit stay human.

 IGoal

Write the goal first.

The intended end state and its invariants go into a document that outlives the conversation. So far: 216 goal documents, 43 campaign plans, 91 ledgers.

 IIPhases

Split into bounded phases.

Parallel agents get non-overlapping scopes. Read-only scouts go ahead of architecture changes; worktrees isolate anything that might collide.

 IIISlice

Implement one coherent slice.

Format, lint, test, inspect the diff—in that order, every time. Weak tests and policy evasion get rejected, not merged.

 IVCommit

Commit as punctuation.

A commit is a cognitive checkpoint between design and the next phase, not an end-of-day dump.

 VAudit

Audit separately.

Correctness, security, performance, and documentation each get their own pass—and goal completion is judged apart from implementation completion.

 The division of labor

Charter and audit (human)

Which problem, which invariants, what counts as done. Architecture and clean-break calls. Whether the evidence is sufficient. Refusal to ship when the audit fails—even when the agents are green.

Coordination and execution (agents)

Dispatch, sequencing, settlement. Reconnaissance, implementation, review passes, documentation.

 In one fleet, 8,452 coordination events ran against 10 that required me. In a separate campaign, an audit caught specs naming tests that did not exist — a naive cargo test would have passed them. The system's job is to refuse, not just to execute.
 216 goals43 campaigns1,396 delivery docs91 ledgers

 The skill library

Make the model’s job easier.

Over the last six months, these repo-owned skills have grown into a cohesive layer of systems-engineering automation with one design goal: make the LLM’s job easier. Nearly every session on this page ran through them.

 Multi-agent loops

/fleet

The newest, and a favorite: Mind, Head, and Hand roles for multi-agent project loops, with stewardship and dead-man continuation. Built on Vivi mailspaces, so agents coordinate over mail instead of shared memory.

 Work-flow spine

/campaign · /factory · /delivery

The work-flow spine, used on practically everything. Campaigns and sub-campaigns organize the flow of work; a factory defines the phases for each unit; every phase gets a ledger that tracks it to completion.

 Per-file loop

/polish

A per-file improvement loop backed by a deterministic analyzer that moves judgment calls out of the model and into repeatable checks. Polish is what keeps boilerplate LLM code from becoming slop.

 Hygiene ratchets

/housekeeping

Repository hygiene with ratchets: not all code is perfect, so exceptions are explicit—and get ratcheted up or down per repo as the code earns it. This is how a codebase stays in clean, competent form.

 Transcript evidence

/cassio

The skill behind the evidence on this page. Converts Claude, Codex, and OpenCode sessions into readable Markdown transcripts—and extracts training data for customized LLM tuning.

 Agent mailspaces

/mail + Vivi

Arbitrary local mailspaces for agents and projects. Vivi grew out of the mail skill and became the substrate Fleet coordinates over—private email treated as durable agent infrastructure.

 …and more

All of it points one direction. The same principle that shaped these skills is the founding premise of Faber: a language designed for LLMs first, because humans don’t write the code anymore—we just need to be able to understand what’s going on.

 The backstory

A career in five acts.

Five acts, dated from executed agreements, payroll records, and public archives where those exist. The evidence ledger below says so when they don’t. Retirement appears once, late—not as the title of the page.

 I1996—2009

Rifles, then a KDE front end for Nmap.

Four years in the Marine Corps—0351 Assaultman, out as a Corporal with an honorable discharge—left me with a bias toward responsibility that never wore off. In January 2000 I released KMap, a C++/Qt front end for Nmap. The Nmap 2.50 release notes mention it by name, which is still my favorite line of third-party evidence.

The path from there was not direct: five years selling real estate in Florida before joining Beatport’s API team in Denver in 2008, where electronic music distribution ran on Zend PHP, enterprise Java, Mule, Spring, Hibernate, Squid, Akamai, and MySQL.

 USMC / 0351 / E-4C++ / Qt / KDEPHP / Java

 II2009—2017

Salesforce, scale, and the founder turn.

At Red Hat I worked on a multilingual APAC Partner Center built on Salesforce—Korea, Japan, and China, twenty-odd sandboxes. roundCorner hired me in 2011 as Chief Scientist; I later held Head of Engineering for a Salesforce-native nonprofit CRM used by large institutions (including St. Jude, Georgetown, Duke). The product line was later acquired by Salesforce.org.

In 2015 I founded Minted.IO and, as a solo founder, built a metadata-driven multi-tenant application platform end to end in six months. After a year at Salesforce as a Technical Solution Architect—forward-deployed with CarMax and Home Depot—Motivis acquired the Minted.IO software/API assets in February 2017. My VP offer was written into the acquisition.

 Chief Scientist → Head of EngFounder / acquiredForward-deployed TSA

 III2017—2021

Platform leadership at scale.

At Motivis I led platform R&D across a team of roughly ten to twenty engineers in an approximately thirty-person company, on a TypeScript, Node.js, and PostgreSQL competency-based learning platform—with deployment portability across AWS, Google Cloud including Spanner, and local environments, and expansion from higher education into K-12.

From 2019 the Motivis relationship shifted toward independent platform and strategy consulting through Minted Geek entities. By 2021 I stepped away from conventional employment. That pause is Act IV; it is not the thesis of this site.

 VP Platform R&D10–20 engMulti-cloud LMS

 IV2021—2025

A short return, then a long pause.

In early 2021 I joined Kraken as Member of Technical Staff on money-movement systems (SWIFT and wire verification). I left after a few months. For about four years afterward I did not take conventional work. In August 2025 the tooling had changed enough that full-time building made sense again.

 Kraken / core eng2021–2025 pause

 V2025—NOW

Full-time lab, measured output.

From August 2025 I returned to full-time independent R&D: Faber/Radix, Minted Geek Swarm, Monk, evaluation harnesses, and the orchestration layer described above. Commit volume and streak data are secondary evidence; the primary proof is falsifiable systems and instrumented process.

In early 2026 I completed Gauntlet AI Cohort 4—a ten-week fellowship at 80–100 hours per week with continuous elimination, delivering production systems each week for three to six hiring partners who evaluated work rather than résumés. The cohort capstone became Cephalopodic with two co-founders; we closed it when managed MCP removed the market.

 Rust / Go / TypeScriptGauntlet Cohort 4Compiler + fleets

 Claims, meet receipts

The evidence ledger.

Old résumés are memory. This history has been reconstructed against executed agreements, employment records, public archives, source code, Git history, and thousands of AI-session transcripts. Sensitive documents remain private; their claims do not. Where the record is thin, the grade says so.

 A — directly verified: executed records, primary sources
 B — corroborated: first-person record plus a credible second source
 C — first-person recollection, not yet independently confirmed

Selected for Cohort 4 of a ten-week AI engineering fellowship in Austin, TX (high aptitude/coding screens; 80–100 hours per week; continuous elimination). Delivered production systems each week against live specifications from three to six hiring partners who evaluated delivered work rather than résumés; completed all ten weeks. Work spanned applied LLM systems and evaluation harness design. Entered already six months into independent full-time R&D.

2025—26Independent AI research at repository scaleA

Full-time independent R&D from August 2025: Faber/Radix compiler work product (hundreds of thousands of lines of Rust, thousands of tests, frequent tagged releases), Minted Geek Swarm multi-agent runtime with measured session economics and audit pipeline, Monk, and related systems. Lab-scale inventories (repos, commits, sessions, trials) measured July 12, 2026 support activity volume; compiler and fleet figures above are the primary technical claims.
